newsitem.title: THAILAND: FOCUS-Thailand floats baht, investors applaud.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Thailand floats baht, investors applaud.

text.p: Thailand floated the baht on Wednesday in a bold move which jolted its stock exchange out of the doldrums and sent shock waves through Southeast Asian markets.
The baht plunged by 15-20 percent in offshore markets despite a bid to offset the blow by the central Bank of Thailand, which raised its lending rate by two percentage points to 12.5 percent.
But Thailand's stock market gave a hearty thumbs-up to the news, with the bourse index soaring by nearly eight percent to 568.79 by the close of trade as foreign firms bought heavily.

Analysts said the tough measures may breathe fresh life into Thailand's ailing economy, which is grappling with a swollen current account, a troubled financial sector and the slowest rate of growth in a decade.

"This is a victory for economic pragmatism over vested political and business interests. The Bank of Thailand finally did the right thing when it had its back to the wall," said Mike Stead of Union Securities Plc in Bangkok.
In offshore currency markets, the baht sank to record lows of around 28.80/29.60 to the dollar from 24.25 ahead of the announcement.
Reaction was mixed around the region, with the Philippine peso and shares falling sharply while the yen surged to 114.15 against the dollar from 114.92 on its perceived safe-haven status.
Analysts saw the managed float as a de facto devaluation allowing the central bank to avoid costly intervention, but said it remained to be seen how far the baht would be allowed to fall.
"The value of the baht will be determined by market forces to reflect fundamental economic forces," finance minister Thanong Bidaya said in an early morning statement.
"The Ministry of Finance and the Bank of Thailand believe the managed float system will benefit Thailand's overall economic development," he said.
Commercial banks would not quote overnight lending rates and exchange trade ground to a virtual halt as markets waited for the central bank to announce its new baht reference rate.
The Bank of Thailand said it would replace its previous peg for the baht, which was set against a basket of currencies, with a daily reference rate based on the previous day's trading levels.
The level will be set at 0130 GMT daily. The Bank of Thailand said it had "an appropriate rate" in mind within which it expected the baht to move, but gave no details.
"However, if the baht goes beyond the appropriate rate the central bank will intervene in the market," central bank governor Chaiyawat Wibulsawasdi told a news conference.

The Thai Bankers Association said local banks had agreed to set a baht trading range among themselves of 75 satangs below and above the baht-dollar reference rate to stem volatility when domestic markets re-open on Thursday.
Analysts said there was a question-mark over how far and how fast the central bank would allow the baht to fall, but they expected it to bring the currency down gradually.
In the near term, higher interest rates would hurt Thailand's economy, but there was scope for them to fall in coming months if the tough measures did ultimately restore confidence.

"There was a tremendous buildup of funds that were waiting to go into the market if there was a devaluation or, as it happened, a flotation," George Morgan, country manager for ABN Amro Hoare Govett, told Reuters Financial Television.

The flotation will allow the Bank of Thailand to avoid intervening to support the baht, after using between four and five billion dollars of its foreign reserves in May to defend the currency from a heavy speculative attack.
This cut the country's foreign reserves to a two-year low of $33.3 billion at the end of May from around $37.3 billion a month earlier
"I think these measures are aimed at boosting confidence," said Kobus van der Wath, Regional Head of Treasury and Economics at Standard Chartered in Singapore.
"But fixing a reference point for the baht allows them to set the pace," he said.
Analysts had expected renewed near-term speculation against the baht because of negative sentiment over the Thai economy and recent moves to rescue its beleaguered financial institutions.

"Under the new system, movements in the exchange rate are expected to be quite large at the initial stage. However, relative stability should be attained after a brief adjustment period," Bidaya said.
Some bankers and analysts warned that Thai corporates with high unhedged foreign loan exposure were likely to face severe repayment problems as exchange costs soared.

Thai corporates have around $60-80 billion or the equivalent outstanding in foreign currency loans, with many unhedged against currency fluctuations after years when the baht was virtually fixed, they said.
"Are Thai companies going to be able to repay their dollar loans is the next big question," one senior European analyst said.
"And if they can't, then the banks are going to have to take a big hit."
Financial authorities have pledged to help businesses hit by the baht's flotation, but there are fears they can do little to help.

With the International Monetary Fund, the Bank of Japan and other central banks also pledging assistance to Thailand, analysts said the future for hard hit Thai firms may come down to the willingness and speed of these agencies to help.
